stated_availability: Two concordant statements, both pointing to a single Zenodo deposit. (1) Data availability statement, p. 10: "The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252." (2) Methods, p. 2: "The entire R code (R Core Team, 2024) used for all the analysis and visualizations contained in this paper is at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252 to enable re-use of materials and improve reproducibility and transparency (Marwick, 2017). All the figures, tables, and statistical test results presented here can be independently reproduced with the code and data in this compendium (Marwick et al., 2018). The R code is released under the MIT license, the data as CC-0, and figures as CC-BY, to enable maximum re-use." Fig. 2 caption (p. 4) adds: "Further details about the model specifications and diagnostics are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252." Recorded descriptively only; no L1-L6 level assigned (L-levels are assigned at reproduction time from actual retrieval attempts, preregistration s7.3).

F1.evidence: Zenodo DOI given as a globally unique persistent identifier in both the data availability statement (p. 10: 'openly available in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252') and Methods (p. 2). DOI form 10.5281/zenodo.14897252 is a valid PID per the PID systems guide (Zenodo, CERN-operated, DataCite registration agency).

F2.evidence: Deposit is in Zenodo, which mints DataCite-schema structured metadata (creator, title, publisher, publication year, resource type, rights, description) for every record; the paper further describes the object as a research 'compendium (Marwick et al., 2018)' with per-artefact rights ('R code ... under the MIT license, the data as CC-0, and figures as CC-BY', p. 2) and points to 'Further details about the model specifications and diagnostics ... at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252' (Fig. 2 caption, p. 4), evidencing description beyond a bare filename.

F3.evidence: The DataCite record generated by Zenodo carries the DOI as its Identifier field, so the metadata explicitly includes the identifier of the resource it describes; the same DOI (10.5281/zenodo.14897252) is cited verbatim in the paper's data availability statement (p. 10), Methods (p. 2), and Fig. 2 caption (p. 4), giving bidirectional paper-to-deposit linkage.

F4.evidence: Zenodo is named explicitly in the instrument's F4 exemplar list ('Zenodo, CRAN, DataCite'). The deposit at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252 is therefore registered in a searchable, machine-indexed resource (Zenodo catalogue, DataCite/OpenAIRE harvesting), not a personal website or unindexed server.

A1.evidence: Retrievable by its identifier over HTTPS via DOI resolution: 'The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252' (p. 10). A1 completeness rule satisfied: coverage_category is 'complete' (6/6 datasets Tier 0-2), so no A1 = 0 trigger. Note (uncertainty flagged, not penalised): the JAS reproducibility-review records behind Fig. 5 concern confidential peer review; the paper states no restriction on them and its blanket claim that 'All the figures, tables, and statistical test results presented here can be independently reproduced with the code and data in this compendium' (p. 2) covers Fig. 5, so they are classed Tier 0 on the paper's own statements.

A1_1.evidence: The access protocol is HTTPS via the DOI resolver to a Zenodo landing page - open, free, universally implementable, with no login, subscription, or proprietary client required. The paper reinforces the intent of frictionless access: data released 'as CC-0 ... to enable maximum re-use' (p. 2). The paper itself (p. 7) characterises Zenodo as 'a non-profit generic research data repository hosted by CERN that accepts any file format and freely assigns all publicly available uploads a DOI to make the files easily and uniquely citable'.

A1_2.evidence: The DOI/HTTPS-over-Zenodo protocol supports an authentication and authorisation procedure where necessary (Zenodo implements closed, restricted, and embargoed access states plus OAuth-token API access). No restriction is needed here - the deposit is 'openly available' (p. 10) and CC-0 licensed - and the protocol nonetheless allows for authorisation should it be required, satisfying the 'where needed' conditional.

A2.evidence: Zenodo/DataCite commit to metadata persistence independently of file availability (tombstone landing pages; DataCite metadata survives object withdrawal), which the instrument's A2 criterion recognises for Zenodo-class repositories. The author's own text endorses this persistence property, contrasting Zenodo with GitHub, which 'does not offer DOIs or the same commitments to long-term availability as Zenodo' (p. 7).

I1.evidence: The deposited data are consumed by R scripts that regenerate every reported output - 'All the figures, tables, and statistical test results presented here can be independently reproduced with the code and data in this compendium' (p. 2) - which evidences machine-parseable, structured representation (R-readable tabular data) rather than unstructured PDF/Word/scanned content. The bibliometric records are structured Web of Science exports with defined fields (number of authors, relative title length, number of pages, recency of references, Shannon diversity of references; Figs 1-3).

I2.evidence: No controlled vocabulary, ontology, thesaurus, or PID-bearing term set is named anywhere in the paper for the data. Bibliometric variables are ad hoc field names following Fanelli and Glaenzel (2013) ('I quantify the number of authors, length of article, relative title length, age of references, and diversity of references', p. 2); no Dublin Core, Getty AAT, PeriodO, ARIADNEplus, or comparable FAIR vocabulary is applied. Unscoreable/absent = 0.

I3.evidence: No qualified (typed) references from the deposited data to other resources via PIDs are evidenced. The upstream source is cited only in prose - data 'collected from Clarivate's Web of Science database' (p. 2) - with no DOI/accession and no relationship type ('isDerivedFrom', 'isSupplementTo') asserted in the paper. The paper-to-deposit link is a one-way in-text citation, not an evidenced qualified reference in the data metadata. Unscoreable = 0.

R1.evidence: Plurality of relevant attributes documented: Methods s2 (p. 2) specifies source database, query, and full derivation - Web of Science category 'Archaeology', Document type 'article' (n = 28,871), filtered to the top-ranking 25 journals by h-index from Clarivate's Journal Citation Indicator, journals with fewer than 100 articles excluded, 'resulting in 20 journals', yielding 'I analysed 9697 papers published during 1975-2025' - plus the five bibliometric variables and their operational definitions; Fig. 2 caption points to further model specification and diagnostic documentation in the deposit.

R1_1.evidence: Explicit, machine-mappable licence per artefact class, stated in-text (p. 2): 'The R code is released under the MIT license, the data as CC-0, and figures as CC-BY, to enable maximum re-use.' Data licence CC-0 maps to SPDX CC0-1.0; this is an unambiguous public-domain dedication, not 'available on request'.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance for the dataset: creation pipeline stated stepwise (Clarivate Web of Science query -> category and document-type filter, n = 28,871 -> h-index-ranked top-25-journal filter -> exclusion of journals with <100 articles -> 20 journals, 9697 articles, 1975-2025; p. 2); analysis software identified ('R Core Team, 2024'); modelling parameters given in the Fig. 2 caption ('For recency of references a Zero-One Inflated Beta distribution family was used with a logit link function ... the Negative Binomial family was used with a standard log link function'), with 'Further details about the model specifications and diagnostics ... available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252'.

R1_3.evidence: The deposit explicitly conforms to a named domain-relevant community standard for computational archaeology - the research compendium specification of Marwick, Boettiger and Mullen (2018), cited in-text: 'can be independently reproduced with the code and data in this compendium (Marwick et al., 2018)' (p. 2). Zenodo deposition additionally applies the DataCite metadata standard, which the instrument lists among qualifying community standards.

F1.evidence: Code carries the same Zenodo DOI persistent identifier: 'The entire R code (R Core Team, 2024) used for all the analysis and visualizations contained in this paper is at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252' (p. 2). This is an archival DOI, not a bare GitHub URL - the distinction the author himself draws on p. 7 when noting GitHub 'does not offer DOIs'.

F2.evidence: Zenodo generates DataCite-schema structured metadata (creators, title, publisher, publication year, resource type, rights) automatically for the software deposit; the paper supplies the licence element in-text ('The R code is released under the MIT license', p. 2) and characterises the object as a research compendium (Marwick et al., 2018), i.e. a structured, described project rather than a loose file drop.

F3.evidence: The Zenodo/DataCite record's Identifier field is the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14897252, the same identifier cited for the code in Methods (p. 2) and in the Fig. 2 caption (p. 4), so the metadata explicitly includes the identifier of the code it describes.

F4.evidence: The code is archived in Zenodo, named explicitly in the instrument's F4 exemplar list, and thereby registered/indexed in a searchable resource with DataCite/OpenAIRE harvesting. The paper contrasts this with unindexed alternatives: 'Most authors are sharing their code and data files via Zenodo, a non-profit generic research data repository hosted by CERN' (p. 7).

A1.evidence: Retrievable by identifier over a standardised protocol (HTTPS via DOI resolution to Zenodo). Coverage is complete for code: the deposit is stated to hold 'The entire R code ... used for all the analysis and visualizations contained in this paper' (p. 2), not a partial subset.

A1_1.evidence: HTTPS/DOI resolution to a public Zenodo record; no registration, subscription, or proprietary software required. The code is in R, an open-source language ('R Core Team, 2024'), so execution imposes no proprietary licence barrier either - contrast with the 'Proprietary software' failure mode the author records for other submissions in Fig. 5D.

A1_2.evidence: The Zenodo HTTPS/DOI protocol supports authentication and authorisation where necessary (restricted/embargoed record states, OAuth API tokens). No restriction is needed for this deposit - it is openly available and MIT-licensed - and the protocol nonetheless provides for authorisation, satisfying the conditional.

A2.evidence: Zenodo/DataCite metadata persists independently of file availability (tombstone pages, DataCite registry). The paper endorses precisely this property as the reason to prefer Zenodo over GitHub, which is 'a problematic choice because does not offer DOIs or the same commitments to long-term availability as Zenodo' (p. 7).

I1.evidence: Code is plain-text R source in a widely shared, formally specified, openly implementable language ('The entire R code (R Core Team, 2024)', p. 2) - a standard, machine-readable knowledge representation rather than a compiled binary or proprietary format. The author's own recommendation reinforces the format choice: 'Code and data files should be in the simplest format possible, for example a plain text R script file' (p. 8).

I2.evidence: No software metadata vocabulary or standard is evidenced - the paper mentions no CodeMeta.json, CITATION.cff, or comparable FAIR-vocabulary artefact for the compendium. Absent = 0.

I3.evidence: No qualified, PID-bearing references from the code to other resources are evidenced. The paper does not state that the compendium contains a dependency lock file, renv.lock, or Dockerfile - despite recommending exactly these to others ('the most robust and widely used include renv (Ushey and Wickham, 2025)', 'authors should use a Dockerfile', p. 8) - so no typed dependency links (e.g. 'uses software [DOI]') can be credited. Unscoreable = 0.

R1.evidence: The deposit is described as a research compendium (Marwick et al., 2018) whose contents are sufficient for third-party execution - 'All the figures, tables, and statistical test results presented here can be independently reproduced with the code and data in this compendium' (p. 2) - and the Fig. 2 caption directs readers to the deposit for substantive documentation: 'Further details about the model specifications and diagnostics are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252'.

R1_1.evidence: Explicit machine-mappable code licence stated in-text (p. 2): 'The R code is released under the MIT license, the data as CC-0, and figures as CC-BY, to enable maximum re-use.' MIT maps directly to the SPDX identifier 'MIT'.

R1_2.evidence: Analytical provenance documented: software identified ('R Core Team, 2024'); the modelling pipeline and its parameters specified in the Fig. 2 caption ('Bayesian Generalized Additive Models were computed to fit the lines summarising the relationships between the variables and the time series ... a Zero-One Inflated Beta distribution family was used with a logit link function ... the Gaussian family ... the Negative Binomial family ... with a standard log link function'), further statistical procedures named in Results (Kendall's coefficient of concordance Wt = 0.64, p = 2.67e-06, Borda Count ranking algorithm, PCA with PC1 = 71 %), and diagnostics deposited at the DOI. Exact package versions/lock file are not evidenced, but creation process, sources, and parameters are.

R1_3.evidence: Explicit adherence to a named community standard for reproducible research organisation in this discipline - the research compendium of Marwick, Boettiger and Mullen (2018), cited in-text at p. 2 ('the code and data in this compendium (Marwick et al., 2018)') and listed among 'excellent, simple, and widely used project templates that authors can choose from that make it easy to follow best practices of project organisation, e.g. Marwick et al. (2018)' (p. 8); Zenodo deposition additionally applies DataCite, listed in the instrument as a qualifying community standard.

barriers: paywall / proprietary (upstream): Clarivate Web of Science bibliographic database - the raw query universe of n = 28,871 archaeology articles (p. 2) - requires an institutional subscription; only the derived analysis dataset is redistributed (CC-0) in the Zenodo compendium, so the upstream source is Tier 2 rather than Tier 0

paywall / proprietary (upstream): Clarivate Journal Citation Indicator h-index rankings used as the journal-selection criterion ('the top-ranking 25 journals according to their h-indices as reported by Clarivate's Journal Citation Indicator', p. 2) are a subscription product - Tier 2

manual extraction: comparative hard/soft values for physics, social sciences, and humanities plotted as the coloured boxplots in Fig. 1 are taken from Fanelli and Glaenzel (2013), an open-access PLoS ONE article, but require manual/table extraction from that publication - Tier 2

manual extraction: the denominator count of JAS research articles published May 2024 - January 2025 (n = 97, p. 7) is a bespoke count from the journal's own listing, reconstructible from the publisher site but not distributed as a standalone dataset - Tier 2

uncertainty (not counted as a barrier): the JAS reproducibility-review records underlying Fig. 5 (47 reviews of 25 manuscripts) derive from confidential editorial peer review; the paper declares no restriction and its blanket statement that all figures are reproducible from the compendium places them at Tier 0, but this could not be verified because supplementary/deposit files were deliberately withheld from this assessment
